chunks.text: II-B Why the forward model must carry the PSF Equation ( 1 ) encodes two assumptions that fail for a fluorescence microscope. First, fluorophores are self-luminous and, in thin specimens, neither occlude one another nor vary with viewing direction, so the occlusion-aware composite collapses to a linear accumulation of emission, I ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = ∑ i e i ​ G i ​ ( 𝐱 ) , I(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\sum_{i}e_{i}\,G_{i}(\mathbf{x}), (3) with e i e_{i} a scalar emission weight. This removes depth sorting and view dependence, making the rendered quantity a measurement of integrated intensity rather than a colour, the same reduction X-ray splatting makes [ 17 ] . Second, the instrument is not a pinhole: the detector records the emission field convolved with the point-spread function h h , I ^ = I ∗ h , h ≈ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , diag ⁡ ( σ x ​ y 2 , σ x ​ y 2 , σ f 2 ) ) , \hat{I}\;=\;I*h,\qquad h\approx\mathcal{N}\!\big(\mathbf{0},\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{xy}^{2},\sigma_{xy}^{2},\sigma_{f}^{2})\big), (4) where the axial width σ f \sigma_{f} far exceeds the lateral one and is a property of the objective, not of the specimen . Since convolving two Gaussians sums their covariances, an emitter of true extent 𝚺 i \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i} is observed with extent 𝚺 i obs = 𝚺 i + 𝚺 PSF . \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\;=\;\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i}+\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{PSF}}. (5) This has two consequences. A model omitting h h absorbs 𝚺 PSF \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{PSF}} into 𝚺 i \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i} , recovering the specimen convolved with the optics and inflated anisotropically in z z . One that includes h h but leaves σ f \sigma_{f} free inherits a non-identifiability instead: shrinking every 𝚺 i \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i} while growing 𝚺 PSF \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{PSF}} leaves I ^ \hat{I} unchanged on every supervised plane, and only planes the model never saw break the tie.

Pinning σ f \sigma_{f} removes that degenerate direction and lets 𝚺 i \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{i} be read as a statement about the specimen. GaussianPile [ 21 ] already encodes a finite-thickness PSF in its projection operator, using the theoretical value. Our renderer inherits that operator and lifts its primitives to 4D under Eq. ( 2 ); what we add concerns the value of σ f \sigma_{f} inside it, where Sec. IV-B finds failure modes on both sides of the theoretical choice. II-E Microscopy reconstruction and evaluation Content-aware restoration [ 38 ] established that learned priors transfer across fluorescence modalities but can hallucinate structure that image-level metrics reward. Putting the PSF inside the reconstruction inverts the classical deconvolution arrangement, where it instead drives an iterative restoration of the acquired volume [ 39 ] ; the constant supplied is the same, and so is the requirement that it be right. Ours is the standard Gaussian approximation to the widefield axial response [ 40 , 41 ] . Sequences and foreground masks follow the Cell Tracking Challenge protocol [ 42 , 43 ] . Image-level SSIM/PSNR [ 44 ] is reported only for completeness; Sec. V-A shows it ranks methods backwards here. III-A Acquisition model A specimen is imaged as a time series of z z -stacks. Under stride k k the robot acquires only frames t ∈ { 0 , k , 2 ​ k , … } t\in\{0,k,2k,\dots\} ; the rest are never measured and serve only for evaluation. Metrics are reported against d d , the distance from a held-out frame to the nearest acquired one. We use two strides, k = 8 k=8 and k = 4 k=4 . The main comparison is at k = 8 k=8 , the sparsest we test and the regime in which nucleus fidelity in the middle of the gap separates the methods most, with a second sequence reported at k = 4 k=4 . No setting is tuned per sequence: the one hyper-parameter that depends on the stride is the gate initialization, which we place at k k frames at both strides (Sec. IV-A ).

Sequences are the C. elegans developing embryo and CHO sets of the Cell Tracking Challenge [ 42 ] . A second holdout runs orthogonally to the first. A subset of z z -planes is withheld from supervision in every run, so that axial extrapolation can be scored apart from fit: the model is fitted on the remaining planes of every acquired volume and evaluated on the withheld ones. Wherever this paper says held-out frame it means the temporal holdout and held-out plane the axial one. Tables I – III report the first; Table IV and the last column of Table V report the second. The forward model splats anisotropic 3D Gaussians and convolves along z z with a Gaussian axial PSF of width σ f \sigma_{f} (Sec. II-B , [ 21 ] ), each primitive gated in time by Eq. ( 2 ). IV Method IV-A Temporal gates in frames, initialized wide A primitive’s temporal extent σ t \sigma_{t} should mean how long this emitter persists, in frames. Native-4D formulations store it as a fraction of the training window, so the same number denotes a fraction of a frame on a short clip and tens of frames on a long one: the parameter describes the experiment’s length, not the specimen. The damage lands where a sparse protocol operates, since on long windows the conventional initialization is an order of magnitude wider than the optimum and the optimizer does not recover. We therefore express σ t \sigma_{t} , its initialization and its learning rate in frames (Table I ). TABLE I: The temporal gate stored as a fraction of the training window ( upstream ) and in frames ( ours ), on a short recording and a long one. Read down a column to compare the two parameterizations at a fixed window length; the bottom row is their difference. The gain scales with window length , the signature of a parameter defined proportionally to that length.

Held-out nucleus flux ↑ \uparrow Training window σ t \sigma_{t} stored as 5 5 frames 100 100 frames window fraction (upstream) 0.934 0.478 frames (ours) 0.970 0.853 Gain (ours − - upstream) + 0.036 +0.036 + 0.375 \mathbf{+0.375} The table separates two things. The absolute level is higher at five frames under either parameterization, because a five-frame window is a nearly static problem in which one primitive can span the whole sequence. The gain is what the reparameterization is responsible for, and it grows with window length, capacity and iteration count held fixed. A by-product confirms the mechanism: the learned gate widths become window-independent and vary with the trajectory a nucleus follows. Where the gate starts matters too, because the optimization is one-directional in practice: gates shrink easily and grow only with difficulty. A gate that is too wide produces visible misalignment and an unambiguous narrowing gradient, whereas one that is too narrow can only widen if the primitive simultaneously learns to move correctly over the longer interval, and per-primitive velocity is not recoverable from sparse supervision. The rule is practical rather than tuned: initialize above the expected optimum and let the optimizer descend. Every initial width at or above the acquisition interval converges to the same solution while smaller ones stall there permanently, so we initialize at the acquisition interval itself, k k frames, at both strides rather than tuning a constant per sequence. IV-B A physical axial PSF The axial width σ f \sigma_{f} has three possible origins and only one is sound. Neither defaulted nor learned.

The conventional data-preparation path assigns σ f \sigma_{f} the z z -step whenever no explicit value is passed, so every prepared sequence carries an axial PSF equal to the plane spacing; across our sequences that overstates the true blur by 1.9 1.9 – 2.3 × 2.3\times , and the reconstruction absorbs the excess by inflating every primitive in z z . Leaving σ f \sigma_{f} free fails the other way: extent and PSF width enter the observation additively (Sec. II-B ), so on supervised planes they are not separately identifiable, and σ f \sigma_{f} duly drifts to 2.74 × 2.74\times the measured value, buying + 0.176 +0.176 nucleus flux for 1.18 1.18 dB of held-out axial PSNR. A wider kernel spreads each primitive over more planes, which an integrated-intensity score rewards and only unsupervised planes punish. Measured, and checked against the optics. We recover σ f \sigma_{f} per sequence from the foreground axial autocorrelation and check it against the widefield prediction FWHM z ≈ 2 ​ λ ​ n / NA 2 \mathrm{FWHM}_{z}\approx 2\lambda n/\mathrm{NA}^{2} [ 40 , 41 ] ; the two agree to within a few percent. The agreement rather than a win is the finding, because it establishes that σ f \sigma_{f} is a constant of the instrument at all, which the metadata default and the learned value are not, and that licenses fixing it. We measure rather than derive because the prediction assumes λ \lambda , n n and NA \mathrm{NA} are correctly logged, and a disagreement would itself be signal that a derived constant absorbs silently. One consequence settles an acquisition-budget question. At the corrected width the axial PSF spans barely more than a single plane, where the default had it spanning more than two, so adjacent z z -planes carry nearly independent information and sparsifying the z z -scan is close to free. The budget should be spent on time.

IV-C Capacity and supervision inside the gaps Splatting methods add capacity where the reconstruction is failing, deciding where from an accumulated per-primitive gradient statistic already known to be fragile on natural images [ 22 ] . Here it averages over every primitive, including the majority whose gate is closed at the sampled timestep and which contribute nothing but denominator, so the longer the window the more the growth signal is diluted: densification behaves normally on a short clip and silently stops on a long one. Restricting the statistic to gate-active primitives repairs it. The growth threshold is the second problem: inherited from natural-image settings, it acts here as a step function rather than a dial, either never firing or running to the primitive cap. Since a representation retrained per experiment needs a predictable footprint, we replace it with an explicit budget, as MCMC-based splatting does for a different reason [ 23 ] , place new primitives at residual maxima, and keep capacity off the background with a significance floor. This buys a knob rather than fidelity: the gate-aware fix alone restores growth. The k − 1 k-1 unobserved timesteps carry no supervision. We supply a low-frequency pseudo-target from 𝒯 \mathcal{T} as a blurred-domain loss: render and pseudo-target are low-pass filtered before comparison, so 𝒯 \mathcal{T} constrains only the band in which it is trustworthy while high frequencies stay determined by the acquired frames. 𝒯 \mathcal{T} takes the two bracketing volumes and the phase between them and regresses the intermediate volume directly, estimating no motion field, because a division is not a displacement. V Evaluation Protocol V-A Full-image PSNR fails on this task We report three independent instances, all on identical checkpoints, held-out frames and masks: (1) Optical-flow warping and the frame-unit parameterization receive opposite rankings under nucleus flux and under PSNR.

(2) Under the old parameterization, at a gate width of 27 27 frames and a nucleus flux of 0.478 0.478 , temporal PSNR is higher than after the fix. (3) Sweeping the σ t \sigma_{t} initialization from 2 2 to 24 24 moves temporal PSNR by 0.42 0.42 dB while the nucleus flux gap across the same sweep is 25 % 25\% . The cause: 92 % 92\% of voxels are background, and warping transports the real, pixel-independent sensor noise that fluorescence denoisers are built to separate from signal [ 37 ] , which a pixel-wise metric instead credits. The remedy is to mask. Masked PSNR is the ordinary 10 ​ log 10 ⁡ ( MAX 2 / MSE ) 10\log_{10}\!\big(\mathrm{MAX}^{2}/\mathrm{MSE}\big) with the error averaged over a foreground mask Ω \Omega instead of the whole volume. That change is decisive here: whole-volume PSNR is dominated by how faithfully empty space is reproduced, so a reconstruction can lose a nucleus outright without moving it. The same holds for SSIM, and a learned perceptual metric [ 45 ] is no remedy either, its features being trained on natural photographs. Every fidelity number is therefore masked: the nucleus metrics by construction, and the z z -PSNR columns of Table IV over Ω \Omega . Whole-volume PSNR/SSIM [ 44 ] is a sanity check. Ω \Omega is the reference segmentation dilated by a few pixels within each z z -plane, never across them: dilating in 3 3 D would let a held-out plane’s mask be defined partly by its supervised neighbours, scoring the axial gap on planes the model was fitted to. Fidelity next to an acquired frame is not what separates the methods; what separates them is how much structure survives to the middle of the gap. We compare against Deformable 3DGS [ 13 ] , a deformation-field method, and 4DRGS [ 20 ] , a native-4D method in the same emission-only regime as ours (Sec. II-A ). Every method is refitted from scratch at both strides under its own published budget policy, with Adam [ 47 ] ; none inherits a model from a denser setting. All arms render through the same PSF-aware forward model (Sec. II-B ) with the same measured σ f \sigma_{f} , not each method’s published optics, so no baseline is penalized for the axial blur its original formulation leaves free and the comparison isolates how each represents time . VI-B Main result: graceful degradation across the gap Table II is the central result; Fig. 2 shows it in plane and Fig. 4 as volumes.

Ours has the flattest decay across the gap, − 46.7 % -46.7\% against − 77.0 % -77.0\% for the next best, and the highest fidelity at every distance from an acquired frame, including the midpoint of the gap, the hardest timestep the robot ever has to act on. Any single cell is within the spread one method shows across seeds, so the slope, pooling all four intervals, is what we rest the claim on. The shape of the curve is the argument, not the height of any one point on it. Beside an acquired frame the methods are close, our lead at d = 1 d{=}1 being a factor of 1.2 1.2 over the best baseline; by the middle of the gap it is a factor of 3.7 3.7 . A method that is adequate at d = 1 d{=}1 and steep thereafter has learned to smooth between observations rather than to model how the specimen moves, and buys a robot nothing. Holding fidelity far from an acquired frame is what the acquisition schedule rewards, because a flat profile turns a longer interval between acquisitions from lost information into saved photon budget. It is mostly the first: ours fits the acquired frames marginally less well than either baseline ( 0.878 0.878 against 0.908 0.908 and 0.906 0.906 ) yet retains more than twice as much of that fit on frames it never saw ( 0.547 0.547 against 0.214 0.214 and 0.258 0.258 ), so the flat slope is not underfitting. Held-out sharpness orders the same way; centroid offset is the one place we trail. Axially (Table IV ), ours and Deformable 3DGS score the same on planes they were fitted to and planes they were not, while 4DRGS scores worse on the withheld ones, propped up by the planes it saw, which is the failure Eq. ( 5 ) anticipates when axial extent is left to the primitives. CHO is the harder test and no method passes it cleanly (Fig. 3 ), because its holdout withholds a larger fraction of planes and the outermost ones; held-out scores are read down a column, never across sequences. However, Ours reconstructs planes it never saw better than any baseline on either sequence ( 12.04 12.04 on CE02, 12.23 12.23 on CHO). We do not read the agreement between a method’s two columns as evidence for the PSF: every arm renders through the same one, and Deformable 3DGS still matches our CE02 temporal representation gap. Whole-volume PSNR and SSIM are not tabulated: they place our arm and 4DRGS within 5 % 5\% of each other and disagree about which is ahead on both sequences, where held-out flux separates the two more than twofold. Their one large spread, 24 % 24\% in CHO PSNR, only restates that Deformable 3DGS is worst. Sec. V-A predicts both behaviours of an unmasked metric on 92 % 92\% background. VI-D Ablation: what the completion signal is worth To isolate the completion signal we compare off , in which the unobserved timesteps receive no supervision, against 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , in which they receive the completion network’s output, at k = 8 k=8 on the frozen clean/quiescent panel ( n = 58 n=58 ) with everything else held fixed (Table V ).

Division-window flux restricts the statistic to nuclei caught mid-division, the events a lineage graph exists to record. Injection raises held-out fidelity with no seed-wise overlap between the groups, and does so precisely where it supervises: the two variants are indistinguishable on the acquired frames they both saw, so the gain is localized to the unobserved timesteps rather than to a generally better fit. It also closes the axial gap , by more than two standard deviations, which is not obvious since the pseudo-targets carry no axial information the acquired frames did not already have: constraining the model in time evidently constrains it in depth. And it makes the outcome reproducible , which for a platform retraining unattended matters more than any mean: on division-window flux the means are nearly identical while the spreads differ ninefold ( ± 0.012 \pm 0.012 against ± 0.111 \pm 0.111 ), so without injection whether a run resolves dividing nuclei at all is decided by the seed. VII Conclusion A robotic microscope is limited by its acquisition schedule, not by its analysis software: the volumes a photon budget will not pay for are the ones its downstream tools assume it has. We have treated those missing frames as a completion problem, fitting a continuous-time 4D state that renders any timestep on demand for the segmentation, tracking and lineage software a lab already runs. Three changes make 4D splatting work at this sampling rate: a temporal gate measured in frames rather than as a fraction of the recording; an axial PSF pinned to a physical constant, which removes a degeneracy the optimizer would otherwise exploit and argues for spending a tight budget on time rather than depth; and gate-aware densification under a budget. What they buy is a reconstruction that degrades gently across the gap rather than only beside the frames that were acquired, and that recovers focal planes it was never shown. Graceful degradation, not peak fidelity, turns a longer acquisition interval into saved photon budget. The natural next step closes the loop in the other direction: using the reconstruction’s own per-timestep uncertainty to tell the robot when the next volume is worth acquiring, as uncertainty-driven view selection already does for where to look next [ 46 ] .
